newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hits 32-month high vs yen as investors leave Japan.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hits 32-month high vs yen as investors leave Japan.

text.p: The dollar rose to a 32-month high against the yen on Monday after comments by Japanese finance officials sent Japanese investors scurrying to find higher interest rates overseas.

Investors sold the yen after Japanese Finance Minister Waturu Kubo said over the weekend that he sees the Bank of Japan (BOJ) keeping short-term interest rates low to ensure gradual economic recovery.
In addition, BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita said the recent decline in long-term Japanese interest rates may reflect changes in sentiment toward Japan's economic prospects.

"Most of it was (Japanese) investment houses ... and institutional investors trying to invest overseas with higher yields," said Jeffrey Yu, senior foreign exchange dealer at Sanwa Bank in New York. "That is what the main push from Japan was."
The Japanese officials were attending a meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven (G7) major industrial nations in Washington over the weekend.
Officials at the G7 gathering went out of their way to avoid unsettling the currency markets, which they believe have achieved a desirable level of stablity in recent months.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated his support for a strong dollar over the weekend and again on Monday.
But the remarks from Kubo and Matsushita were given added weight on Monday by data showing Japan's industrial activity fell 1.9 percent in August.

In Tokyo on Monday, the dollar powered above 111.20 yen, the previous 1996 high set in July. It reached 111.68 yen -- its highest level since hitting 111.75 in January 1994 -- before settling back to 111.37 yen in New York, up from 110.90 late Friday.
The yen slid broadly, retreating against the German mark and reaching its lowest level versus the British pound since May 1993.
The dollar also rose to 1.5291 marks early Monday -- its highest since July 8 -- before slipping to 1.5250 marks in late trading, versus 1.5244 late Friday.
The British pound rose to $1.5650 from $1.5637.

Japanese interest rates are the lowest of any major nation, prompting Japanese investors to shed yen-denominated assets more actively than their counterparts in countries like Germany are shedding assets denominated in their local currencies.
This has given the dollar more of a lift against the yen than the mark.
"It's just nominal yields," said Mark Gargano, foreign exchange manager at First Union National Bank. "You've got 0.50 percent (deposit rates) in Japan and you've got 3.0 percent in Germany."
There is more money coming out of Japan going into investments in the United States, Canada and Britain, than coming out of Germany, Gargano said.
The yen may have received an extra shove amid speculation that capital will flow out of Japan more freely in the second half of the Japanese fiscal year, which starts Tuesday, traders said.
"Customers from Tokyo just had to buy dollars after the old fiscal half-year," said Yu.
Japanese overseas investors and businesses often sell dollars to repatriate yen for accounting purposes before the conclusion of their fiscal accounting periods in September and March.
Once the new accounting period starts they are free to sell yen again.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.2545 Swiss francs from 1.2565 Swiss late Friday and it rose to Canadian 1.3620 from C$1.3632.
